utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are awaiting the arrival of Mr. Deronjic. I gather there's a matter which the Prosecution want to raise. Before you do so, let me deal with the programme for the rest of the day. We've considered the accused's request for more time. On this occasion we will allow it. The accused can have three-quarters of an hour. The amicus, a quarter of an hour. The proposal, the objective being to finish the witness by the adjournment. We will then hear Witness C-057. We will admit his statement under Rule 89(F). We would urge on the Prosecution a minimum of examination live so that the accused can have the balance of the day to cross-examine that witness with a view to finishing the witness. We will sit -- since we're starting late, we will sit a little longer, at least until 2.00, but we have to be out of the court for a hearing at 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that helpful indication of the programme and I'll communicate with Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff about C-057. Your Honour, there are -- apart from the one matter that I've indicated through the usual channels, I wanted to raise, there are also some other 92 bis packages that can be tendered. Perhaps it would be better to do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do that now so that it is in fact done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first one is B-1010, 92 bis (A) granted on the 22nd of July of 2003 without cross-examination, the package to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 602.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next one is Mirsad Pajic or Palic. 92 bis (A) granted on the 10th of October without cross-examination, the statement to be tendered publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we have the name again for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Palic, P-A-L-I-C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: According to my document it seems to be Talic -- you're quite right. My error. I've got the wrong one. Yes, Mirsad Palic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 603, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next one is Sead Kurbegovic, 92 bis (A) granted on the 31st of October without cross-examination. One 92 bis statement to be tendered publicly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 604, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next one is B-1499, 92 bis (A) granted on the 31st of July without cross-examination, the statement to be tendered under seal. And then --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 605, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then finally B-1516, 92 bis (A) granted on the 22nd of July without cross-examination. The statement to be under seal, but three of the attachments at tabs 2 to 4 can be tendered publicly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Finally, Your Honours, 606.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, a couple of other procedural matters to help the Chamber and all the participants. Obviously as we reach the end of the year, filling the remaining days is always problematic, and we seek to give the maximum advance notice of what's likely to be called. We understand there's still uncertainty about the date of the 9th, and so that week there may only be the one sitting day. If there is the one sitting day at present advised, we will call Mr. Markovic for that -- or recall Mr. Markovic for that day, and we'll have to fit everything around him. I'm not excluding the possibility of a telephone call next week to see if we can accelerate him into the -- into next week but I don't think it's likely. I think he will be coming on that day, the 10th. Working around that and recognising that I can't mention publicly all the witnesses, there may be a gap next week because of witnesses who have been allowed without cross-examination, and we're not in a position at the moment to know who for sure we can pull forward for those days. The material of an OTP witness, Dean Manning, is going to be served today but it comes with a large amount of supporting material and we doubt if he's somebody who can be introduced next week, although if all the parties agree that can happen. There's the in-house witness Tore Soldal, who is somebody who has been allowed to be added to the list, and he's somebody who we might call actual notice in the absence of any sustained objection if a gap develops. But at the moment, the uncertainty about the 9th of December doesn't make it difficult but it obviously adds to the logistical difficulties of getting witnesses, and I think it will be that we'll not call the witness listed on the 9th of December, on the 10th of December we'll call Mr. Markovic and fill in the time as best we may. As to Mr. Markovic, the Chamber required him to come back to conclude his cross-examination, and I think used a form of words that said, "Your examination will conclude on the day you return," without specifying precisely how much time in further cross-examination was to be allowed. If my recollection on that is correct, it may be that all parties would find it helpful to know roughly how much time is to be allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Give me the date on which he gave evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, coming up. 23rd of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have here and my note is that the accused is to have three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In which case in reality that will consume the whole of the day if the accused wants to use his three hours, because the amici will have some questions, I forecast, of such a witness, and there will be a little bit of re-examination, or may be. There is going to be an urgent application for protective measures for one of next week's witnesses. It will be with me by, I believe, 10.00 so I will have it for you before the break. Your Honour, the only other matter I was going to raise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you go on to that, let me deal with one other administrative matter about next year and the sittings next year. The week of the 13th of January, in fact the first week back, we shall not be sitting on Wednesday the 14th, but we'll change that to Friday the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must ensure that there is a court available then. I'd be grateful if court management could be informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only other matter that I'd like to raise perhaps I could raise in private session in substance.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Kwon raises the possibility of starting C-057 as a possibility so we wasn't waste yet further time. It may be that the best course is for us to rise for a few minutes to try and see what's happened. But if Mr. Deronjic isn't here and we have 20 minutes or so, it might be an idea to at least start that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll make arrangements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll rise now. --- Break taken at 9.39 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In order to make as good time as we can of the time available, we will sit now for two sessions with a half-hour break between them. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before I begin, Mr. May, with regard to your time restriction on my cross-examination, since you told me to select from this extensive statement of 240 paragraphs the relevant parts, I would like to remind you that when I do so, I hear from the side opposite that I should have challenged what I wanted to challenge, and I challenge everything here, and I want to make this clear for the record before I start my cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: To make it also clear for the record this: You will not be criticised if you are subject to time restrictions and you don't put every single point in your case. Clearly that will not be right, and you won't be. But we also take account of the fact, and I think it's fairly plain, that you challenge everything in the Prosecution. Yes. Now let's begin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I'm taking into account, because I challenge everything in the Prosecution case, "Prosecution" being the term that you use.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deronjic, let us just finish discussing your meeting at Pale. Allegedly you had a one-on-one talk with Karadzic first, informing him about the situation in general, and later you informed him about Beara's visit. Look at paragraph 213, where you discuss the situation in general, the prisoners, the transport of civilians. In the same paragraph, you say that 2.000 Muslims had been transported -- sorry, 20.000 Muslims had been transported, and you say, "I conveyed to him my impression that everything had been executed properly, without incident, at least as far as I knew. These people were taken to Kladanj." Kladanj was then controlled by Bosnian Muslim forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You told him it passed without any incidents and the people had been taken to Kladanj. Tell me, why didn't you ask Karadzic on that occasion if he had really sent Beara?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I quoted to President Karadzic precisely what Beara told me in my office on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You told him about the visit of Beara probably in the same terms as you did it here, that he had come drunk, that he made a racket, and you quote only one of the things he said, like "These soldiers are fools." This does not mean that you asked him if he had been sent by Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 214, when you conveyed something from Borovcanin about liquidations on the road from Konjevic Polje to Kasaba, you say: "I remember he told him that the retaliation by our people was inspired by something they had done." Is it clear from that that there was no order that they should be killed but he, rather, interpreted it as an act of reprisal on the part of people from Srebrenica in retribution for the crimes previously committed by Naser Oric and his forces?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not dispute that it may be your conclusion. I dare not draw any conclusions on the basis of the very few facts that I have at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm only quoting you here.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I didn't draw that conclusion. He commented on the events in the Kravica cooperative, and he told me, "Well, this can be seen as a retribution, as payback for the incident created by the Muslim forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 216, you say: "Once I returned to Bratunac, I saw a lot of buses with the prisoners were gone. I inquired where they had gone and I was told they had been taken to Zvornik." So obviously neither you nor he knew at the time, because this is something you thought after talking to him, you thought that somebody had killed those people, or at least some of them.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct. I didn't know at the time that those people had been killed. I conveyed to him the intentions that I understood were held by the army, or at least what was conveyed to me by Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that on the 15th or the 16th you broached the subject of evacuation from Potocari, which gave you a reason to visit the UNPROFOR base where you met the commander, Mr. Karremans, his assistant Mr. Franken, and others. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you explain how you drew up some sort of record together with them where you wrote that evacuation is being handled correctly.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Although I don't have this report by Mr. Franken, I noticed that there is a handwritten note made personally by Mr. Franken which says that everything had been done properly, but that applies to the convoys escorted by the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he confirmed that the convoys handled by the UNPROFOR had been carried out properly, but he couldn't say anything about the other convoys.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, you were informed that there had been some killings.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you did not inform them. You concealed it from them.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the UNPROFOR? Mr. Milosevic, the document you are referring to, the record of evacuation of civilians from Potocari, refers only to that evacuation from the Potocari base. According to the information I had at the time, those civilians had not been mistreated. They were transported instead to Kladanj. That record applies only to the transport of civilians who had been at Potocari at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Deronjic. Throughout that meeting with your delegation from Srebrenica in Karadzic's office, which according to the document I tendered lasted from 2.25 to 6.25, that is four hours, what did you discuss for four hours?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic -- in fact, Mr. Milosevic, there were two segments to that meeting. I don't know exactly how the meeting lasted. In the first segment, I had a tete-a-tete with Mr. Karadzic, and that relates to the information which I summarised in my statement. The rest of the time we discussed the fact that my position, that of the civilian commissioner, was abolished. It was transformed into the War Presidency. I was president of the War Presidency. We had to agree on the composition of the War Presidency and a number of other topics that included the normalisation of return of displaced persons and refugees to Srebrenica, and many other related topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You speak about the return of refugees to Srebrenica, the normalisation of life, the establishment of this War Presidency, but you were president of the War Presidency in Bratunac; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was the year 1995. After occupying the post of civilian commissioner for only three or four days, it was renamed into War Presidency, and I was appointed president of the War Presidency in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But before that you were president of the War Presidency in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That president of the War Presidency was the most important person in that area, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And throughout that time while you spoke, while you discussed the normalisation of life in Srebrenica, the return of refugees, it was never mentioned that some people had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That meeting was attended by some ten people from Srebrenica, some of which I myself didn't know very well. I explained to the Office of the Prosecutor how this meeting had come about. It was precisely at the request of those people. It would not have made sense, and it would have been indiscreet to discuss such topics in front of strangers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "strangers"? Those were people from Srebrenica who came to attend the same meeting as you did. Is it possible that they were not aware of anything, having come from that locality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you think that President Karadzic and I would discuss in front of them things like Beara's visit to my office and the orders he conveyed to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I saw the notes you made about the visit of Beara to your office and those alleged orders he had conveyed to you. I just want to be clear on this point: You did not discuss anything of the sort at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the presence of those people from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I would now like to ask you only a few questions related to spring 1991. On the 9th of March, 1991, were you in Belgrade for the demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you took part in those demonstrations, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were even on the podium, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I applied to address the public, but I didn't get a chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And those demonstrations were organised -- those were the first violent demonstrations in Belgrade in 1991, organised against the authorities and against me personally, and you were a participant, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with your qualification that they were violent but they were organised against you and your government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that was on the 9th of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And only a couple of months before that multi-party elections were held where I was held -- where I was elected president with an overwhelming majority and where the Socialist Party won more than an overwhelming majority in the Assembly. At the time, you were an official of the SDS, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you took part in the demonstrations against the government in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then immediately after those demonstrations, you came to Belgrade, straight to the Presidency of Serbia, and as you claim here, you went to see Kertes; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it was immediately after. It was the end of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In any case, in the month that followed.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you asked for a personal sidearm, you say that he sent you to the MUP, and you say also that some hand grenades were put in your cars for some sort of drills. Is that what you asked him for?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We asked -- in fact, Zekic asked if we could get some weapons for personal use. Kertes called somebody in the MUP and they gave us two hand grenades each.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't get any sidearms, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us come back to the demonstrations of March 1991 in which you took part. Do you remember, Mr. Deronjic, from that time that those volunteers who were gathering there all came from the opposition parties that had organised the demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which volunteers are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All the volunteers that you had occasion to see there and whom you brought to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it was not me who brought them. Second, they had come through the government bodies of the Republic of Serbia. Their membership in opposition parties is something I'm not aware of. I suppose you may be referring to Seselj's men or maybe some other opposition party. I didn't get involved with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The main organiser of those demonstrations set up the Serb Guard, the Serbian Renewal Movement, as you well know.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And all these people you enumerated were representatives of opposition parties.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you consider Seselj and his party opposition, then that's true. I don't agree with that personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was indubitably in opposition.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In your opinion maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you were on good terms with them, unlike the authorities. Is that true, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not true, Mr. Milosevic. With parties such as radicals, Jovic's party, whatever its name was, I was on no terms whatsoever. On the contrary, it was you who had a coalition with then. I had a relatively good relationship with Vuk -- Vuk's party.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The party of Vuk Draskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the year 1991, 1992, 1993. At that time, I had no coalition with any of the these parties, and that is easy to establish. But let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's not move on straight away. What you're saying is true, but you did form a coalition with those parties later, and I was on no terms whatsoever with then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the fact that you participated in demonstrations against me together with them.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic and Mr. Seselj did not take part in those demonstrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is well known who did take part and how, but let's not waste any more time. What position was Kertes occupying when you came to visit him in his office?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the man for the first time then. I didn't inquire about his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know that either?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your statement here was worked out in a very systemic manner, precisely the way this side opposite is trying to portray everything that happened. I will try to go through these things as soon as possible. So let us look at paragraph 4 and the heading: "Illegal arming of Bosnian Serbs, Spring 1991." And then in paragraph 4, you talk about Goran Zekic who was a member of the Bosnian Serb Republic Assembly. You call them the Bosnian Serbs. I don't know what you are.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a Serb, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they're Serbs too. And then you move on to say: "He told me that he was obtaining weapons through smuggling channels --" that's what it says here in paragraph 4 -- "and he even mentioned the name of the person through whom he was procuring it. It was a man who was a Muslim from the Zvornik area. On one occasion, I went with him to buy a rifle for myself." Is that what you wrote?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't write it; that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's what's written in that statement of yours. So through smuggling channels when you talk about the arming of the Bosnian Serbs in the spring of 1991, that is how these weapons were obtained. And as a matter of fact, even from a Muslim that you bought a rifle from.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you move on to say that there was a meeting with Rajko Dukic, a certain businessman, as you describe him. And towards the end of paragraph 6, you say: "This was a man that had very high political standing in Belgrade and among the leaders of the SDS." Where did he have this very high political standing in Belgrade? With who in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I found out during the war and later that he had good relations with the SPS and JUL at the time. I did not check that. I did not have the possibility of doing so, so I allow for the possibility that perhaps this was not the case. In the previous period, this man did have certain positions in the business and political circles of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You should know as an SDS official, Mr. Deronjic, that the SPS, the Socialist Party of Serbia, never had any relations with the SDS. It was an opposition party.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Serb Democratic Party. The Socialist Party of Serbia never had good relations with the SDS. As a matter of fact, they had no relations. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. On the contrary; at all the rallies that you held against the opposition, the SDS took part as well. And I even sent a telegram of protest protesting that. Also, I witnessed many meetings between you and leaders of the SDS, and I know of them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My contacts with Karadzic and Krajisnik were contacts with officials of the Republika Srpska, not the SDS. They were officials of Republika Srpska. One was the president of the republic, the other one was president of the Assembly. Krajisnik was also president of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as you know.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now you mentioned JUL and that this Rajko Dukic had good relations with JUL. Well, you know that JUL was established in 1994, so he could not have had any relations with JUL that did not even exist then.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that he had good relations in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what year was this then, please? If you are talking these particular years here, then what was the year when he had good relations with JUL, and what kind of relations could he have had with then anyway?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is it that precludes the possibility of him having any relations with them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't even say whether it was 1994 or 1995 when JUL was founded, but let's not go into all that. He had no relations with them whatsoever. I mean, that is completely false.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how did he know about Mr. Kertes then?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know about him having been with Kertes at all. Or do you have any evidence to prove that? I have noticed in your statement that all the people whose names you mention in terms of having had tete-a-tete meetings with them in Serbia, all of them are dead. Isn't that right, Mr. Deronjic? None of them can corroborate what you've said.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kertes is not dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so you had relations with Mr. Kertes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I came to see him. I came to see Mr. Kertes, which was on the recommendation of Rajko Dukic. Of course, I do not have an influence over events. I was not a person who staged the death of anyone. Goran Zekic was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How was he killed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, he was killed by the Muslims, and if you're interested in that subject, I have the complete documentation here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to go into that subject.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be good to go into that subject if you want to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's not waste time. Mr. Deronjic, we are under constraints of time, so if you could try and avoid arguing with the accused and just stick to your answers, please. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 8, you say that Dukic, whom I don't know, told you that a decision had been passed to arm the Serbs, and then he told us, you say, and I quote - and all of this is a quotation from your statement, I'm quoting you - paragraph 8: "Karadzic personally convinced Milosevic the Serbs are to arm themselves." And further on you say: "They did not believe that the JNA could protect the Serbs. Karadzic wanted to arm the people." Mr. Deronjic, even the birds that fly know that Belgrade, Serbia, and I personally supported the JNA. Don't you know that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this is completely wrong. Why would Karadzic need my approval to arm himself? I don't command the JNA. What does this mean? You say here that he convinced me that the Serbs should arm themselves. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. Mr. Dukic exactly used that sentence. Later on, when I had a meeting with Karadzic, I heard that very same sentence, that he personally convinced you that people in Bosnia, primarily meaning the Serbs, should arm themselves. And he explained this by saying that he had no confidence in the army, the Yugoslav People's Army, and he thought that at a critical point in time they would not defend us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And my position was completely opposite, that the JNA should be supported. I am sure you know that.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not that I know most of these things, but if that's what you claim --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then in paragraph 6, you say about Dukic, that he was involved in different affairs, even some criminal dealings, and that he was well known for having done that, and you say that he was notorious for having been involved in such criminal affairs, et cetera. So you believe that.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe anything. I just quoted what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then in paragraph 10 you talk about your return to Bratunac. Goran Zekic said to you that he knew people that were involved in the army. So these are some officers who helped with the arming, and he said that Veselinovic was the person in charge of that entire operation. Who was Veselinovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Veselinovic a few times. I don't know his name. He died. He's one of the founders of the SDS and one of the greatest financiers of the SDS at the outset.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Veselinovic is dead and Goran Zekic is dead; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many people are dead, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Regrettably, yes. And then you say that Kertes was trying to impress you, that he mentioned Croatia and even Kosovo. What did Kosovo have to do with anything going on in 1991? Was anything happening in Kosovo then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I quoted what he had said. He boasted that he took part in the arming of Serbs in Croatia and in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did Kosovo have to do with anything in 1991 and the arming of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to ask him about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And even you say that allegedly he asked you whether you wanted to visit me, but then you didn't have time and therefore you didn't visit me. Doesn't that seem a bit -- a bit -- how should I put this? Doesn't this seem like an illusion altogether, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in my statement that I did not know whether this was possible, but he alleged that you were in that building, and that was his proposal, and I said that there was no need for that and there wasn't any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not challenging that, that I was probably in the building where my office is. There's no doubt about that, because you claim that you entered the building of the Presidency of Serbia, and at that time I was the president of Serbia, so I was certainly in my office if I was not elsewhere at that particular moment.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you like me to describe Kertes's office for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's no use. I have no use for that. I personally could not remember what his office looked like, although it was in my building. And you claim that he was there then, but at that time he held no position, no office in the Presidency. He was not a member of the -- he was, rather, a member of the Presidency of Serbia until 1990, until the elections were held, but then according to the new constitution, Serbia got a president, not a Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Milosevic, that at that time Mr. Kertes was having dentures made?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assure you I have no recollection of that. And then you say that in -- in paragraph 17, you say it was you and this late Zekic who cannot confirm that, you said that this is an area 50 kilometres from the Drina River, and he was saying that everything would be Serb within that area of 50 kilometres from the Drina River. He, a Hungarian, is saying that everything in that area of 50 kilometres from the Drina River will be Serb. Who could say that? I mean, even a Serb. Who could say anything? I mean, a person who knew anything of history and geography could not say that and you're claiming that Kertes told you that.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that that is what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say something about Bubanj Potok that belongs to the military. Do you think that Kertes was in a position to issue orders to the army?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously he was, because the arms from Bubanj Potok not -- came not only to Bratunac but also to other municipalities precisely from Bubanj Potok.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is very questionable. You say that you saw a truck being loaded allegedly while you were there, and you asked what this was and then one of the soldiers said that these were weapons going to Croatia. The assumption is that this was the JNA and that at that time there was a regular JNA operation there, nothing else. Isn't that right, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please, in paragraph 21 you say -- I mean, you keep on talking about this Zekic all the time, and you say all the time -- well, let me not quote everything. He said that he would organise the transport himself, that this would be his task, and that he should arrange the transfer and that "we should find people to transport the goods in Bosnia itself. And he said that I should find several people in Bratunac whom I trusted ..." Isn't quite clear here that this is smuggling?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no way of transporting weapons to Bosnia legally. There was absolutely no way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course there was no way of doing it legally. Look at your next page or, rather, paragraph 26. You say: "Soon after that, Slavko Jovanovic arrived, who had already prepared a spot where the weapons would be kept. And soon thereafter, Rasa Milosevic arrived with Milan Sundjin, and they all told me that they had prepared sites, locations in Serbia along the Drina where they would keep the weapons and later on transfer them to Bosnia." And then you say: "He designated a place in his friend's weekend cottage in the village of Bacevci, which is across from the village of Patovici," so that weekend cottage in Bacevci is in Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then these other two men, towards the end of this paragraph, you say: "He found some premises in a co-op called Velika Rijeka, in a cooperative." That is in Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he found a weekend cottage in Serbia and also an agricultural cooperative, the premises of an agricultural cooperative. So this was a clandestine business altogether. How can you say that it was the MUP of Serbia that approved of this if you are hiding this in a weekend cottage in the area of Serbia and also in some agricultural cooperative in the territory of Serbia? Why would this have to be hidden from the MUP of Serbia if the MUP of Serbia had approved of this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I will tell you why I claim this. The truck that arrived in Ljubovija around that time -- I just remember that that was when the soccer finale game was held --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just keep it short. I mean, soccer.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this truck was stopped in Ljubovija. This is where a Muslim worked, at the police station in Ljubovija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ljubovija is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Serbia, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A Muslim worked in the police in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And this Muslim suspected that there was some kind of smuggling going on and that's why the truck was there, and the rest of the police removed this man and advised Goran to move on to Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were present there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many policemen were there in Ljubovija? In Ljubovija there would have been two policemen who could have stopped a truck or perhaps even one only. I assume that this wasn't a group of policemen there.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A two-man patrol?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: One was a Muslim, one was a Serb, and then the Serb told the Muslim to go away, removed him, and then advised this man to go on further?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Zekic went to the police station in Ljubovija, and then the situation became completely different. This man was removed, this patrol was removed, and Goran Zekic went on to Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He probably did this on the basis of some personal connections of his then. Isn't that obvious to you, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you think that Goran Zekic commands the police in Ljubovija, then that would be about right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's no command, it's a personal connection.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he can change patrols on the road?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think he could change patrols. And also you say in paragraph 27, rather 28, "And then people were saying that I was the one who had done that and transported the weapons." So you did it.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I participated in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, not participated. People knew that you had done it. You say: "I had done that, that I had transported the weapons." That's what you say. "This was the first transport in the area, and then after that, I was no longer directly involved in such matters."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way in which I described this, I mean there's no need for me to repeat that. I described exactly how the weapons had reached Bratunac. I personally did not transport it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I'm quoting you. You say, "I did it." You always use the first person singular, and obviously this is smuggling. And you also talk about an army depot, and then before that you say that you don't have any confidence in the JNA. Doesn't all of this seem quite contradictory to you, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, I did not say that I did not have any confidence in the JNA. Secondly, at the moment when the political crisis in Yugoslavia became very radical, we all practically knew that there would be a war, because there were more important objectives than political objectives. That was the need for us to protect ourselves, to defend ourselves in that area, and it is for those reasons that I went to get these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But when you describe how all this came about -- let us make a small digression. In paragraph 44, and you will remember this for sure immediately because you were involved in politics, you say, "The Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 14th and 15th October 1991, in the absence of SDS deputies, passed a memorandum supporting the creation of a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Serbian side in Bosnia-Herzegovina accepted even the idea of Bosnia and Herzegovina separating from Yugoslavia provided it was cantonised, and even in 1992, before the outbreak of any conflict, the Serbs accepted the Cutileiro plan, as it was called?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that. I remember every detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these reactions that you refer to were reactions of the Serbian side to the referendum which excluded them from deciding on their own fate. Is that true, Mr. Deronjic, or not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true, Mr. Milosevic. And in one of the paragraphs, I described it precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was not the Serbs who made a plan to separate themselves. It was, rather, that they were excluded from deciding through a referendum.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. Milosevic, but the Serbs did make a plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you are talking about Variants A and B. It was a public document of the SDS. But tell me, Mr. Deronjic, under the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were Serbs a constituent people in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when they were excluded from the decision-making process in Bosnia and Herzegovina, they organised themselves in order to survive.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were my motives too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we're not talking here about some plan they made to secede or separate themselves from others. They were planning -- making plans to protect themselves. And you know, Mr. Deronjic, that the first armed attacks in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina were attacks against Serbs. Is that true, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know these facts very well. I can't answer this question. There were attacks from both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment so the witness can deal with it. The suggestion is that the Serbs were making plans in order to protect themselves. That's what the accused is putting. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I explained how I came to learn about that plan, the plan for creating Republika Srpska. In April 1991, I learned for the first time that there may be a division of Bosnia in the future. In the beginning, as it was publicly explained, this plan implied division by political means, namely that we would create our own political entity using political means. In the beginning of 1991, I understood, however, that the objective was to join Serbia and that it was also planned to use such means as expulsion, killing, et cetera. That's what I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Deronjic, what kind of killing and expulsion are you talking about in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And concerning your references to division, don't you know that even the Cutileiro plan, which involved an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, envisaged that it be divided into cantons, some of which would be majority Serb, majority Muslims, others majority Croat? Don't you know that? This was common knowledge. Your representatives negotiated this with others at international conferences on Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Cutileiro plan did exist. We accepted it. I know that well. However, the creation of Republika Srpska did not result from the Cutileiro plan, because that plan fell through. It was a different project altogether, as I have explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You need not explain any further. Let us come back to the arming. You say in paragraph 29 that weapons were arriving from the army in Tuzla, and all that was organised by Goran Zekic, whom you referred to in the beginning. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, him, among other people. I also mentioned Mr. Jankovic, if I am not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say some General Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant Petar Jankovic right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ah. Petar Jankovic. I can't find him at this moment. Is Tuzla in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is Tuzla located in an area populated mainly by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that Tuzla remained under Muslim control throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You go on to say, and this is all the year 1991, that there was a General Djukic, commander for logistics. Are you talking about the late General Djukic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I'm talking about the Uzice Corps now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that there was some Marko Milanovic in Skelani at the time, a representative of the structures. I don't think this is your vocabulary, Mr. Deronjic. What it says here is he was from the structures in charge of arming Serbs. I don't think that's the kind of language you use.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why don't you believe that? It's a geographical term denominating Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These people were in Australia. I never heard Serbs using the term "Bosnian Serbs."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs from Bosnia or Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you are the first Serb that I hear calling Serbs Bosnian Serbs. You say that he wasn't there in the beginning, he came later.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before -- just before the beginning of the war in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did he come from?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the police. As far as I know, from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In any case, from Bosnia. He was from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I only wanted this clarified. And then you say it was not necessary to procure weapons from Serbia because a large depot of weaponry had been established in Milici; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the bulk of the weaponry was procured from Milici, which is not far from where you lived; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you speak about the arming of Bosnian Serbs, as it says here, by the JNA, and you say it was an activity engaged in by the Territorial Defence. The Territorial Defence in your own area; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, if you mean Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I mean Bosnia. It was through the Territorial Defence. And then you go on to say: "I know very little about the organisation of Territorial Defence. I know their headquarters were in Tuzla." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "I knew that, because my brother-in-law worked in the TO, and he was engaged precisely in the training of young people." And then you speak about the fact that your brother-in-law, Milenko Stjepanovic, was killed in the war. And you say that the training took part in a school in Rujevici and he was in charge of the training of those young men in your area; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 34, you say: "Muslims boycotted the army including even the Territorial Defence, which at the time was part of the JNA. So the Muslims boycotted the army and the TO, and a couple of lines below you say they organised training for Serbs only because the Muslims did not want to participate any longer. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the Territorial Defence did not expel the Muslims. They boycotted the TO, and the Territorial Defence was composed of those who didn't; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it's -- the Serbs did not expel Muslims from the Territorial Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's now 11:00. You can have ten minute more. That will have given you practically three and a half hours to cross-examine this witness. So you've got ten minutes more now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be very difficult for me to complete this within ten minutes. I'll try to skip a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Milosevic. Since you haven't finish this topic of the Territorial Defence, can I add a comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very briefly, please, because time is short.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say that it was not our practice with regard to normal drills of the Territorial Defence for the weapons to be kept by those involved in the exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to clarify what you wrote here: "That the Muslims boycotted the army. They boycotted the Territorial Defence, that training was organised for Serbs because the Muslims did not want to take part." Those are indisputable facts, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say -- I'm skipping quite a lot of these paragraphs. I'm skipping to the part where you mentioned Bijeljina, Zvornik, Visegrad. You know at least from information which became available later that the fact that Arkan's Volunteer Guard was there, and we heard a witness here who said there were 20 men of that guard, came because they were paid to do so, and they came to Zvornik in exchange for 400.000 Deutschmark at the invitation of the local leadership. They were paid for that job, and they had nothing to do with the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I know very well who is in the leadership of the SDS in Zvornik. It was not true that they were paid or invited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, very briefly, if there is something you want to add, you can, but it must be short.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I always keep thinking that Mr. Milosevic will follow-up on his questions. I want to say that the leadership of the SDS in Zvornik was arrested when Arkan arrived. They were tortured, mistreated, and kept in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Even they didn't testify about that. However, you are not testifying about Zvornik, and I don't want to waste my time on this. Please, in paragraph 56, you say: "I asked Goran Zekic what it was all about and why I had been called to come. He told me that he had brought volunteers there." So he brought volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't it you together with Zekic who brought the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Some of these volunteers are still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In any case, he brought them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what you say. And the volunteers, as you -- we established, were organised by various parties.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And Zekic brought them there.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the Territorial Defence in Bajina Basta, with the assistance of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that there was some sort of scheme, some sort of pattern. First the volunteers would arrive - we just established who brought them - followed by killings, and then the JNA with an apparent desire to restore order. You are saying that the JNA was pretending they were establishing law and order. You know how many places they came to to restore order, and you call this a pattern?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Milosevic, because it was your scheme. Instead of arresting volunteers, as I insisted, they arrested me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't insist on anyone arresting the volunteers. You brought the volunteers, and the JNA tried to restore order.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I have a document dated the 13th of May that testifies that I expelled volunteers from Bratunac. I have a document about this. The JNA refused to do it, so I did it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Deronjic. You probably expelled some men you had a personal conflict with. You certainly didn't expel any of the volunteers that you had brought yourself. And then you go on to conclude, in paragraph 68, in the way Mr. Nice is trying to represent it here, the creation of Republika Srpska, a very serious move, when they were expelled by that referendum, they proclaimed the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the MPs in the parliament did.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did so in the Serb parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you explained that the creation of Republika Srpska was a complex and serious move that had to have been planned in advance. Didn't we just establish that the Serbs were sidelined by that referendum and had to take measures for their own protection? They were shunted to the margins.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're mixing up dates. We were talking first about the beginning of the 1991. That was followed by Serb activities to establish Serb autonomous regions. The parliament verified them at the session of the Assembly in November, and that was followed by Variants A and B, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will not go into what the SDS did, but the Serbian autonomous regions were formed spontaneously for the purpose of self-protection.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an order of the SDS to establish them, and they were verified by the Assembly in November 1991, and that was done publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Publicly, of course. They made it quite public that that is the way in which they were protecting themselves from the violence that they were exposed to. They were establishing Serb autonomous provinces. Everything was done in public. So this was not done in any planned fashion. There was no plan whatsoever let alone a secret plan. This appeared everywhere, wherever they felt threatened or jeopardised. Tell me, what does this mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer that. Was this done publicly, Mr. Deronjic, as is alleged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The establishment of Serb autonomous regions was a public affair. Their verification in the Assembly in November 1991 was also a public matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please just comment, Mr. Deronjic, on paragraph 72 briefly. What do you say there? You say: "I sat there with Miodrag Jokic." Miodrag Jokic is not the general that is referred to here. This is some local person of yours down there.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "When one man in uniform asked Ljubisa Simic whether he was president of the municipality." So this was a man in uniform, someone from the JNA. "And I also remember him saying to Ljubo Simic that he should compile lists of all extremists, both Serbs and Muslims."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the representative of the JNA asked him to compile a list of extremists, both Serb and Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wait a moment, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just reading what you wrote here.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is it written that he's a representative of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say a man in uniform. Usually when a person says "man in uniform," they usually mean the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, way. These are volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He told you to compile a list of all extremists, both Serbs and Muslims, and Ljubo Simic was very tense and soon thereafter he left the meeting. He said, and then you quote: "I'm not going to take part in this. If you want a list of Serb extremists you should put my name on it first, on the list." Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does this have to do with somebody's activity aimed at preventing conflicts, at having tensions abate? Who are these people who asked to be informed about extremists from both sides between who there could be a clash?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are volunteers, and their intention was not to prevent a conflict at all. Soon afterwards they caused a conflict as they killed Muslims in Bratunac, as they looted property, so many activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These volunteers that you brought.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, but you say that Zekic brought them. So Zekic brought these volunteers who then looted and killed there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And Zekic is dead. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have two minutes left now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I really don't know, Mr. May, I mean, whether there's any point in all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if you want to use the two minutes, you can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a look at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The arrival of the JNA in Bratunac. That's what you say. And you talk about some 20 men, members of the JNA, and we heard evidence here that they were commanded by a certain Lieutenant Musa, who was an Albanian. And you say that this was the Novi Sad Corps. However, you yourself say that these people had arrived from Sekovici. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sekovici?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, by way of formation, establishment, army district and corps were not limited in any way by republican boundaries. This was a unit that was stationed in Sekovici but was also in Bosnia-Herzegovina, right in your neighbourhood; isn't that right? And you yourself say they same from Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to me what was this that happened? What happened? You say Glogova. That's a sub-heading here. It was my understanding of this document that you concluded a plea agreement with this so-called Prosecution, and you agreed to testify, and now it seems that you disarmed the inhabitants of this place called Glogova; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that the Yugoslav People's Army worked with the approval of the Crisis Staff and that they disarmed the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army disarmed everyone, but let's clarify this. You say here in paragraph D of this indictment of yours -- and you pleaded guilty to all of it, so as far as you're concerned, it is not contested, but as far as I am concerned, I have an opinion of my own, and I believe it is shared by everybody else in this regard. You say: "Milutin Milosevic, chief of the Serb SUP, told the villagers of Glogova that they would not -- that Glogova would not be attacked because they had turned over their weapons. This Milutin Milosevic added that he was speaking on behalf of Miroslav Deronjic." So on your behalf, you were president of the Crisis Staff, he was speaking on your behalf, and he said to the inhabitants of Glogova, which is almost a purely Muslim village, that they would not be attacked because they had handed over their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Where are you reading this from?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm reading from paragraph D of this -- well, I got this entire set of documents. This is your plea agreement with the Prosecution, that you would testify, that you would plead guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's the passage in the indictment itself. It's paragraph 8(D).

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Paragraph 8(D). Exactly, Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it is my understanding that Mr. Deronjic confirmed all of this.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So on your behalf, the chief of the SUP, Milutin Milosevic, informed the inhabitants of Glogova that they would not be attacked. And already in the next paragraph, paragraph (E), it says: "Miroslav Deronjic in his capacity as president of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Bratunac, a position which gave him de facto and de jure control over the TO and de facto control over the police gave an order ..." That's what it says here, "... gave an order to attack the village of Glogova, burn part of it down, and forcibly displace its Bosnian Muslim residents."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, time will run out and you won't allow me to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I'm just reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time. Mr. Deronjic, have you got the passage that the accused is referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Milosevic is reading the indictment, and he claims that I admitted to all of this. But in the text of my plea agreement, this is not what is written down. And the accused is insinuating that I pleaded guilty to all of this and that that is what is written, the other text, the plea agreement, and that, quite simply, is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I really do not have time now to go back with you to this very voluminous document, but in the agreement itself that you made with this Office of the Prosecutor so that they would propose a lower sentence for you and that -- and in order to have that done you agreed to testify against anyone that they asked you to testify against, that agreement invokes the second amended indictment that I am quoting from. And by way of this agreement, you accept this second amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So how can you say that what I'm reading from this second amended indictment, which you accepted and signed through your plea agreement, both you and your lawyers, and now you say that this is not true?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's true or not, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm sorry. You're reading very fast, and time is running out, and it seemed to me at one moment, because it's so hard for me to follow, that you were saying something that I had not agreed to, but now I've read it, yes it's true, that's what's written here, that Milutin Milosevic did say that he was speaking on my behalf, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us clarify what is in the indictment. Would you look, please, at the two allegations which are in the indictment which is attached to your plea agreement. You will see the passages to which the accused refers, paragraph D which says that Milutin Milosevic, speaking on your behalf, told the villagers they wouldn't be attacked because they had turned over their weapons. Do you accept that as being true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I accept this absolutely as being true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Then the next paragraph reads that you, in your capacity as president of the Crisis Staff, a position which gave you control over the TO and the police of Bratunac, gave an order to attack the village, burn part of it down, and forcibly displace the Bosnian Muslim residents, and that you were aware that you were ordering an attack on an unarmed civilian village. Now, is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. It is completely right, Your Honour. May I just explain briefly in one sentence what I meant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You needn't worry about time, you can explain exactly what you mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milosevic previously spoke and insinuated that I or somebody else had disarmed the Muslims. I said that the action of disarming the Muslims was based on a decision passed by Mr. Reljic. So this was the plan of the JNA, his plan, and that is how the disarming of the Muslims took place in Bratunac. It is correct that I said that the Crisis Staff agreed with this decision to disarm the Muslims. As for the action of disarming the Muslims, it was Mr. Reljic who was in charge of it, and I thought that Mr. Milosevic was insinuating that, that I passed this decision and that I carried out the disarming of Muslims in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with anything, and I'm not insinuating anything. It is quite clear that here, on your behalf, the chief of the SUP, who is under your command, informed the inhabitants of Glogova that they would not be attacked and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need to repeat it all. We've read that. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I cannot finish, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, because you've made the point and we can read it, and the witness accepts that it's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, Mr. May, my point is that this witness concluded an agreement with the Prosecution, the Office of the Prosecutor, in order to be able to lie here on behalf of the Prosecution and for the benefit of the Prosecution. That is the core of this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with that because it's right that, the allegation having been made, the witness should deal with it. You've heard what's said, Mr. Deronjic. What's said by the accused is this: That you have come here to lie on the basis of a plea agreement, an agreement you've made with the Prosecution. That's a very serious allegation, and you should have the opportunity of dealing with it. Is it true or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do thank you, Your Honour, for giving me this opportunity. I think that I did not insult Mr. Milosevic at any given point in time. As for every count --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't take it for these purposes as an insult. The important point is that the allegation has been made and you should answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is absolutely not true. I am testifying here, and I said that during the sitting yesterday, that my absolute wish was to testify before this Court and that that wish has nothing do with the agreement that was concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have decided to deal with two subjects only, and they will only have to do with the contacts between Mr. Deronjic and Mr. Karadzic and General Mladic. This is contained in his statement, because he did not have any direct contacts with Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deronjic, I would not want to go back to paragraph 181 that you dealt with extensively yesterday, but what you say there in that part of your statement, and that is what needs to be explained to the Trial Chamber primarily, you said inter alia that Karadzic had said to you: "Miroslav, all of them need to be killed." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you said -- and then you explained this in paragraphs 185 and 187, that on the 11th, that is to say two days after this meeting with Karadzic that was held on the 9th, you heard on the radio that you were appointed civilian commissioner for Srebrenica and that Karadzic told you in a telephone conversation what was envisaged by that office. Was this a normal telephone conversation? Is that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a normal telephone conversation, and that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 187 you said that you insisted on the following, that you be given the decisions that were passed and that these decisions be faxed to you, if possible. Are those the decisions that were faxed to you? Have you seen them until now? I'm not sure that they were exhibited before this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've already shown you this book. These are all the war orders issued by Karadzic, and that's where I found these orders with the seal of Republika Srpska and the signature of Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are these the two decisions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have them in English as well, Your Honour. They were translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If we could have them, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, I have seen the first decision, which has to do with my appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had this decision in my possession, and it is correct, this is the one I received. As for this other decision, this is the first time I see it. I never had the opportunity of seeing it earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell us whether the core of this matter is to respect war orders and to especially protect the civilian population? Was that the essence of these two decisions?
